description:
File browser, terminal, text editor and admin toolkit for Windows. Install or run portable. GPLv3. No account, no agent, no telemetry.

KillerShell puts a file browser, a PowerShell or CMD terminal, a text editor and an admin toolkit in one window, on one tab strip and one set of keys. Search any folder by filename wildcard or by file content, streamed live with no index to build. Processes, services, performance and the registry are one key away. Runs portable or installs for you or every user - no runtime, no agent, no account. Open source under GPLv3.
1.6.2 makes clicks respond right away again, gives This PC drive tiles with usage bars, puts program icons in the Processes list, and fixes the Trash Polka tool pages and the 98SE look.
Fixed
- Clicks respond right away again. The window draws on the graphics card and falls back to the CPU only under Remote Desktop or a screen-sharing agent.
- Making a new folder in the file picker no longer freezes the window on a share that stopped answering.
- A This PC tab restored from the last session lists the drives instead of opening empty, and shows the computer icon in the tab strip.
- The Performance page wraps on a narrow pane and its cards scroll to the page's foot, so nothing runs off the edge or gets cut off.
- At 110% and 125% app size the active tab joins its page without a line, with the tabs above or below.
- With the tabs at the bottom, the active tab under search results matches the status row it joins instead of showing a lighter face.
- On the 98SE theme the active tab's corners are square, so the neighboring tab's outline no longer shows as a black dot beside it.
- The footer's pane layout buttons stay visible after a click instead of filling in solid, and 98SE drops the extra divider beside them.
- An untitled document's card and tab list row show a text document icon instead of a white dot, and its title lines up with the other cards.
- On the 98SE theme the Performance page has a clean tab-page edge instead of a striped border of stacked gray lines.
- Under Trash Polka the Performance page, the Storage map, the file picker, drop-down lists and flyouts show the theme's surfaces and ink instead of flat or too-dark fills.
- On 98SE the title bar buttons, tabs, menus, dialogs, window frame and icon rail match Windows 98.
- Confirm and quit dialogs size to what they say, so a short prompt like Quit is narrower.
- With the tabs below, a list that scrolls has its bottom shadow back.
- On 98SE with the Yellow accent, turned-on card tiles show dark text instead of white on yellow.
Changed
- The tray icon's card shows the KillerShell logo over one row of tiles, Open and then Exit, like the other cards.
- Under Trash Polka outline buttons have a solid dark face with white text.
- The document bar's settings gear opens a tile card like the other cards. The reading options flip in place and keep it open, and Indent picks its width from a list.
- The document bar's encoding picker opens a tile card with one tile per encoding, the current one filled.
- The Export button opens a small card with CSV and HTML tiles and their shortcuts.
- Storage's depth and minimum-size pickers open tile cards with the current value filled.
- The search scope chooser opens a tile card, with a fourth tile for searching within the current results.
- The terminal profile picker opens a tile card with a tile per profile and one for managing them.
- A card with exactly four tiles shows them in one row instead of three and one.
- The Trash Polka Yellow accent is a bright yellow with dark text on selected rows and turned-on tiles, instead of a brownish gold.
- The Performance card's wide setting reads Multi-column, since a wide card spans every column.
Added
- The Performance page lays its panels out three columns across when it is at least 1200 pixels wide.
- This PC shows each drive as a tile with a usage bar and its free space, as Explorer does. The bar is green, turns yellow at 80% full and red at 95%.
- The Processes list shows each program's icon beside its name.
- Swedish and Korean interface languages. Both start as machine translations for native speakers to refine.
